clue.text: Perhaps Crufts dog commercial cut

parts.note: to dog someone is to follow them closely, as a shadow does
a commercial is an advert, AD for short

explanation.surface: A dog-show advert at Crufts has been dropped.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing AD from SHADOW leaves SHOW. 'Dog' is a verb here, not the animal the Crufts surface suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: Crufts is a famous annual dog show held in Britain, so it is an example of the general word.

clue.text: Maybe 10 o'clock breaking news up (per Tim Ewart)

indicators.note: a breaking word is split open, so the target is buried across the words that follow

parts.note: found running from the end of the first word into the start of the last

explanation.surface: A late-night news bulletin presented by the ITV reporter Tim Ewart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Breaking news' is a fixed phrase on the surface, so the split between its two words is easy to miss.
explanation.definitionFit: Ten in the evening could be when someone has their late meal, an example of the time.

clue.text: Ninth bloke out not running properly

indicators.note: out here means out of order, so the letters are disordered

parts.note: the letters of these words, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: The ninth man in a race has dropped out and stopped running.
explanation.definitionFit: A machine on the blink is faulty or working erratically, an informal idiom.

clue.text: Type of lamp that guaranteed a broad smile?

parts.note: a deal that is guaranteed is sealed
to beam is to smile broadly; a beam is a broad smile

explanation.surface: A question about a lamp that could be relied on to make someone grin.
explanation.definitionFit: A sealed-beam lamp is a headlamp unit in which the reflector, lens and filament form one sealed whole.

clue.text: Date finally settled with English woman

indicators.note: finally points to the very end of the word, so only its closing letter counts

parts.note: last letter of date
dust that has settled has lain down
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A wedding date has at last been agreed with an English bride.
explanation.definitionFit: Elaine is a woman's given name, so any woman could be named this way in crossword terms.

clue.text: DPhil, say … fancy title

parts.note: the letters of these words, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A doctorate, for instance, counts as a grand title.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' reads as 'for example', but its letters are part of the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: Ladyship is a form of address for a woman of noble rank, as in 'Her Ladyship'.

clue.text: One bristled at being described as very silly?

parts.note: surface reading: someone who took offence at a description; setter's reading: a thing with bristles, used in a simile for foolishness

explanation.surface: Someone took offence at being called extremely foolish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bristled' means took offence on the surface, but literally means having bristles, pointing at a household cleaning tool.
explanation.definitionFit: The British idiom compares a foolish person to a broom, meaning thoroughly silly or scatterbrained.

clue.text: An elite college, West Point has regular expulsions

indicators.note: throwing out at a steady interval means every other letter is dropped

parts.note: the even letters of these words, the odd ones expelled

explanation.surface: The American military academy keeps throwing out cadets.
explanation.walkthrough: Eton is the famous English public school near Windsor.
explanation.definitionFit: Eton College is one of England's most exclusive fee-paying schools, educating many prime ministers.

clue.text: The compiler sets vacuous shambles

parts.note: the setter referring to themselves

indicators.note: vacuous means empty, so the inside of the word is cleared out and only its ends survive

parts.note: first and last letters of sets

explanation.surface: A setter admits to producing an empty-headed muddle.
explanation.definitionFit: A mess and a shambles both mean a disorderly, chaotic state of affairs.

clue.text: Compassion — mine and yours primarily

parts.note: a pit is a coal mine

indicators.note: primarily means in the first place, so only the opening letter of the word is used

parts.note: first letter of yours

explanation.surface: Someone offering sympathy that belongs to both of us.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mine' looks like a possessive pairing with 'yours', but it is the noun: a coal mine.
explanation.definitionFit: Pity is sorrow felt for another's suffering, a close synonym of compassion.

clue.text: Sugary confection — clean teeth after Charlie (with his brother?)

indicators.note: after says the teeth-cleaning word follows the nickname rather than leading

parts.note: Charlie is slang for cocaine, and nose candy is another nickname for it, a sibling term

explanation.surface: Instructions to brush your teeth after eating sweets with a boy named Charlie and his brother.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracketed question hints that CANDY is a relative of Charlie: both are slang names for cocaine.
explanation.definitionFit: Candy floss is spun sugar wound on a stick, sold at fairs; Americans call it cotton candy.

clue.text: Carrot and thyme mixed with first drop of oil — it's delicious in a salad

indicators.note: ingredients mixed are stirred together, so their letters are jumbled

parts.note: the letters of carrot and thyme

indicators.note: the first drop is the opening bit, so only the initial letter is taken

parts.note: first letter of oil

explanation.surface: A recipe: carrot and thyme with a dash of oil make a tasty salad.
explanation.definitionFit: Cherry tomatoes are small, sweet tomatoes commonly eaten whole in salads.

clue.text: A big beast, Brazilian legend knocked back Hampshire ale freely

indicators.note: a drink knocked back is downed, but here the name is sent backwards
letters arranged freely are not held in their printed order

parts.note: Pelé, the Brazilian football great
HANTS is the standard abbreviation for the county of Hampshire
the word ale, rearranged

explanation.surface: A football legend downing lots of beer in Hampshire, a county in southern England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knocked back' suggests drinking the ale, but it acts on the footballer's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Elephant seals are the largest seals, the males weighing several tonnes, so they are fairly called big beasts.

clue.text: Some ketchup in a cola, dad? That's a rum drink!

indicators.note: some means a portion of what follows, so the letters are taken from within those words

parts.note: running from the last letter of ketchup to the start of dad

explanation.surface: A child asks their father if he has put ketchup in his cola, calling it a strange drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rum' means odd on the surface, but it is the spirit.
explanation.definitionFit: A piña colada is a cocktail of rum, coconut cream and pineapple juice.

clue.text: Fresh UK leader? That is capital north of the border

indicators.note: something fresh is new, so the letters are made into a new word

parts.note: the letters of these words, to be rearranged
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, that is

explanation.surface: Speculation about a new British prime minister, with a reply naming a Scottish city.
explanation.walkthrough: North of the border means Scotland. Auld Reekie, Scots for 'Old Smoky', is a nickname for Edinburgh.
explanation.definitionFit: Edinburgh is Scotland's capital and has long been nicknamed for its smoky chimneys.

clue.text: Rows involving 50 roofers

indicators.note: something involving another takes it in, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: tiers are rows, as of seats
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: Fifty builders on a site squabbling with each other.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rows' reads as quarrels, but it means lines of seats.
explanation.definitionFit: Tilers lay tiles, including roof tiles, so roofers are people doing that trade.

clue.text: Pud from America — I spoil it on the way back

indicators.note: going on the way back means travelling in the opposite direction, so the string is read right to left

parts.note: the United States
taken as written
to mar is to spoil
taken as written

explanation.surface: An American worried they will ruin a dessert while travelling home.
explanation.walkthrough: Pud is British slang for pudding, meaning dessert.
explanation.definitionFit: Tiramisu is an Italian dessert of coffee-soaked sponge and mascarpone, a sweet course.

clue.text: Writer half the month sat on table

indicators.note: half of a word is its first four of eight letters here

parts.note: the first half of November
a table is a list of figures

explanation.surface: An author spent half the month sitting on furniture.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down answer the first piece sits on top of the second, hence 'sat on'.
explanation.definitionFit: A novelist writes novels, a specific kind of writer.

clue.text: According to Spooner, rabbit takes the mickey out of rhino kept here

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner was famous for swapping the opening sounds of words

parts.note: a bunny is a rabbit; it takes the opening sound of the other word
to take the mickey is British for teasing, to mock; it takes the opening sound of the first word

explanation.surface: A rabbit poking fun at a rhinoceros in a zoo enclosure.
explanation.walkthrough: Rhino is old British slang for money, so the animal is a red herring.
explanation.definitionFit: A money box is a container where cash is saved, so it is where rhino, slang for money, is held.

clue.text: Manager ran department charged with a commission

indicators.note: something charged with a load carries it inside, so the letters sit within these words

parts.note: found across the ends and start of these words

explanation.surface: A manager who ran a department was accused of taking a kickback.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charged with' suggests a criminal charge and 'commission' a bribe; both are misleading.
explanation.definitionFit: An errand is a task one is sent to do for someone else, which is a sense of commission.

clue.text: Not about to punch card immediately

indicators.note: a punch drives into something, so one piece is driven inside the other

parts.note: an ace is a playing card

indicators.note: turned about means facing the other way, so the word runs backwards

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone refuses to strike an awkward character straight away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not about' looks like a single phrase meaning absent, but 'about' acts on 'Not' alone.
explanation.definitionFit: At once means without delay, an idiom equivalent to immediately.

clue.text: Rock famously carved Sister Tharpe's sound

parts.note: Sister Rosetta Tharpe, the American gospel and rock-and-roll pioneer, with the possessive
a tone is a sound, especially a musical quality

explanation.surface: Praise for a singer whose sound shaped rock music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rock' looks like the music Sister Rosetta Tharpe helped create, but it is a stone slab.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rosetta Stone is an inscribed granodiorite slab whose carved texts unlocked Egyptian hieroglyphs.

clue.text: Pine tree trunk felled around noon

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so one piece wraps the other

parts.note: a felled tree trunk is a log
N is the abbreviation for noon

explanation.surface: A pine tree was cut down at about midday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pine' looks like the tree, matching the surface, but it is the verb meaning to yearn.
explanation.definitionFit: To pine for something and to long for it both mean to yearn.

clue.text: Ambush magistrate without hesitation

indicators.note: without in its old sense means outside, so one piece encloses the other

parts.note: JP, Justice of the Peace, is a magistrate
um is a sound of hesitation

explanation.surface: A justice of the peace is attacked without a moment's pause.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without hesitation' reads as 'promptly', but 'without' means outside.
explanation.definitionFit: To jump someone is to attack them suddenly, which is to ambush them.

clue.text: Generous hands holding uniform large releases of eggs

indicators.note: hands holding something grip it inside, so other letters go within

parts.note: a generous round of applause, a big hand, is an ovation

L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: Kind helpers clutching a large school uniform.
explanation.walkthrough: To give someone a big hand is to applaud, so hands here are rounds of applause.
explanation.definitionFit: Ovulation is the release of an egg from the ovary, so the plural fits this phrase.

clue.text: Fire old Russian cavalryman after leaving function

indicators.note: what is left after something leaves is the remainder once that part is gone

parts.note: the Cossacks were famed horsemen of the Russian steppes
cos is short for cosine, a trigonometric function

clue.text: A ghetto pod cast that describes Terry-Thomas?

parts.note: the letters of these words, to be rearranged

explanation.walkthrough: Terry-Thomas was a British comedy actor famous for the wide gap between his front teeth.
explanation.definitionFit: Terry-Thomas's trademark was a prominent space between his front teeth, so the adjective portrays him.

clue.text: Grand prix perhaps featuring electronic vehicle reversing

parts.note: E is the usual abbreviation for electronic, as in e-mail
a car is a vehicle

explanation.surface: A motor-racing event in which an electric car backs up.
explanation.definitionFit: A grand prix is a top-level motor-racing event, an example of the general word.
